name: First Try Matters: Revisiting the Role of Reflection in Reasoning Models
authors: Liwei Kang, Yue Deng, Yao Xiao, Zhanfeng Mo, Wee Sun Lee, Lidong Bing (lead affiliation: MiroMind AI; with National University of Singapore and Singapore University of Technology and Design)
venue: arXiv preprint (cs.AI); also indexed as DBLP CoRR abs/2510.08308. A version is under double-blind review on OpenReview (id g6xbW1FFXf), consistent with an ICLR-style submission.
reflection_object: reasoning chain (the post-first-candidate portion of a long chain-of-thought is analyzed; the paper analyzes/categorizes the model's reflective reasoning trajectory rather than modifying output content, and for its proposed method it truncates the reasoning chain at inference time). It does not introduce a new corrective intervention; it is an analysis of native reflection plus an inference-time early-stopping controller over the reasoning chain.
requires_training: SFT (for the analysis experiments, SFT on Llama3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; the proposed early-stopping uses two small trained Qwen3-1.7B classifiers — a Candidate Answer Detector and a Question-aware Reflection Controller. The headline efficiency method itself applies no gradient update to the base reasoning model)
reward_or_critic_model: verifiable reward (correctness of candidate answers judged by the rule-based Math-Verify verifier during analysis; for the early-stopping method, two trained Qwen3-1.7B binary classifiers act as controllers rather than reward models)
distillation_target: none (the paper does not distill reflections into a reusable artifact; SFT experiments distill DeepSeek-R1/Qwen3-8B rollouts into student weights only to study the effect of reflection amount, and find gains come from first-answer correctness, not stored corrective skill)
emergent_vs_engineered: Analysis of RL-emergent reflective behavior in o1/R1-style reasoning models (both RL-trained and SFT-distilled). The paper's own contribution (question-aware early-stopping via CAD+QRC controllers) is engineered/scaffolded on top of that emergent behavior.
error_localization_granularity: step-level (a long CoT is segmented into reasoning steps delimited by line breaks; an LLM-based extractor locates the positions of candidate answers, and reflections are defined as the content between two consecutive candidate answers; correctness transitions T->T, F->F, F->T, T->F are classified at the candidate-answer step level)
intra_task_vs_inter_task: intra-task (the analysis concerns refinement/reflection within a single question's reasoning trajectory; the early-stopping intervention also operates within one task at inference time; there is no cross-task experience transfer)
failure_recovery_vs_avoidance: post-hoc-revision (the studied native reflections are post-first-answer revision attempts, found to be predominantly confirmatory and rarely corrective; the paper's intervention truncates rather than recovers)
benchmarks: AIME2024, AIME2025, AMC, OlympiadBench, MATH500 (analysis over 3,427 rollouts per model; SFT evaluated on the combined set of these five)
headline_result: Question-aware adaptive early-stopping (CAD + QRC) on Qwen3-8B reduces reasoning tokens by 24.5% across five math datasets (15,125 -> 11,414 avg tokens) with only a 2.9% average accuracy drop (84.7% -> 81.8%); CAD alone gives 29.9% token reduction at a 3.8% drop.
baselines: Native full-reflection generation of the reasoning models (e.g., Qwen3-8B with full reasoning); CAD-only early-stopping (terminate at first candidate) as an ablation vs CAD+QRC; for SFT studies, cut-at-i datasets (cut-at-1 through cut-at-6) and varying ratios (0%-100%) of corrective (F->T) reflections; before-vs-after RL comparison (MiroMind-M1-SFT vs MiroMind-M1-RL at 7B/32B).
gains_vs_baseline: Efficiency: vs full Qwen3-8B reasoning, CAD+QRC cuts tokens 24.5% for a 2.9% accuracy drop (CAD-only: 29.9% tokens / 3.8% drop). Tunable trade-off: 1pp accuracy drop -> 12.0% token reduction; 8.12% accuracy drop -> 40.7% token reduction. Analysis findings: reflections after the first candidate consume 16.8%-47.8% of tokens but add only 1.4%-3.5% accuracy; >90% of reflections are confirmatory and corrective F->T reflections are mostly <2%. SFT: cut-at-6 beats cut-at-1 by 4.05% avg accuracy, of which +3.75% is from first-answer correctness and only +0.3% from reflections. RL gains come mainly from first-answer accuracy (+4.6% for 32B, +7.7% for 7B) with reflections contributing only +0.3%/+0.1%.
compute_cost_profile: The proposed method REDUCES inference compute: ~24.5% fewer reasoning tokens (CAD+QRC) or ~29.9% (CAD only) vs single full-reflection pass, while staying within ~2.9-3.8% accuracy. It adds two lightweight Qwen3-1.7B classifiers (CAD scores each generated sentence; QRC scores the question once). Training-side cost in the analysis: six SFT datasets each fixed at 28M tokens (cut-at-1 has 6,754 questions, cut-at-6 has 3,405 questions); corrective-ratio study uses ~6K problems; SFT run on Llama3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.
known_limitations: Scope limited to mathematical reasoning (five math benchmarks) and to reflections occurring after a first candidate answer; the LLM-based candidate extractor is imperfect (94% human-judged correct on a 100-rollout/426-candidate sample); reflection-type analysis relies on Math-Verify rule-based checking; the early-stopping incurs a real accuracy cost (e.g., -5.8% on AIME2025); QRC/CAD are tuned with specific thresholds (0.05 / 0.5) and the trade-off is dataset-dependent; findings about reflection being confirmatory may not generalize beyond math or to non-reasoning-model LLMs.
oracle_or_external_feedback_dependency: oracle-label/ground-truth — the analysis labels each candidate answer's correctness with the ground-truth-backed Math-Verify rule-based verifier to classify confirmatory vs corrective reflections. This is the discriminating variable: the paper SHOWS native reflections rarely flip wrong->right (corrective F->T mostly <2%), i.e., intrinsic self-correction is weak; the efficiency method does not require an oracle at inference (it relies on learned CAD/QRC classifiers).
self_correction_efficacy: net-negligible/confirmatory — native reflections are predominantly confirmatory (>90%) and rarely corrective (F->T mostly <2%); subsequent reflections add only 1.4%-3.5% accuracy while the first answer dominates final accuracy. Training to add corrective reflections does not increase the model's flip probability p(F->T) (best-vs-worst difference only 1.7%). Self-correction efficacy is therefore essentially marginal/task-dependent, with first-try correctness being the real driver.
calibration_effect: not-measured (the paper does not directly study confidence calibration; it studies answer-correctness transitions and token efficiency, finding reflections are mostly confirmatory rather than examining over/under-confidence)
failure_attribution_capability: classifies-failure-mode (taxonomy) — proposes a taxonomy of reflection transitions between consecutive candidate answers: T->T, F->F(same), F->F(diff), F->T (corrective), T->F (degradation), with T->T and F->F(same) defined as confirmatory and F->T as corrective.
failure_mode_addressed: Targets/exposes superficial or 'confirmatory' self-reflection (reflections that merely reaffirm an existing answer rather than correcting it) and the resulting overthinking/redundant-reflection token waste; relates to MAST-style superficial self-reflection and overthinking/redundant-reasoning modes. It also documents a counterintuitive mode: models reflect more on easy problems and less on hard ones (reflection budget misaligned with task difficulty).
builds_on: DeepSeek-R1 (RLVR reasoning models), OpenAI o1, Chain-of-Thought prompting (Wei et al. 2022; Nye et al. 2021 scratchpads), inference-time scaling work (Snell et al. 2024; Muennighoff et al. 2025 s1; Brown et al. 2025); uses MiroMind-M1 (Li et al. 2025) SFT/RL data and models, Qwen3, gpt-oss, MiMo-7B-RL, Magistral, and the Math-Verify verifier; conceptually relates to critiques that self-reflection is superficial (Liu et al. 2025).
reasoning_model_native: true — the paper specifically targets o1/R1-style reasoning models with built-in reflective reasoning (analyzes 8 such models: MiMo-7B-RL, gpt-oss-20b, Magistral-Small-2506, DeepSeek-R1-0528, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, Qwen3-8B, DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B) and argues their gains come from first-answer correctness rather than reflection.
on_policy_distillation_link: Tangential. The SFT experiments distill DeepSeek-R1/Qwen3-8B rollouts into Llama3.1-8B/Qwen2.5-7B students and find more-reflection rollouts mainly raise first-answer accuracy (via diverse-path exposure), not corrective skill — implying that what gets distilled is improved first-try competence rather than a self-correction routine. Not framed as on-policy distillation, but informs OPD/skill-optimization debates about whether reflection is a transferable skill.
sample_efficiency: Analysis scale: 3,427 rollouts per model across 8 models (AIME2024/2025 32 rollouts per question, AMC 4, OlympiadBench and MATH500 1). SFT: six datasets fixed at 28M tokens each (cut-at-1 = 6,754 questions, cut-at-6 = 3,405 questions); corrective-ratio study ~6K problems. Early-stopping controllers (CAD, QRC) are Qwen3-1.7B trained on annotated MiroMind-M1-SFT rollouts. Human-eval robustness: 100 rollouts / 426 candidates, 94% correct.
